name: Fatima Schmidt

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or any party. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I translate German, Arabic and English, mostly from a desk by the window in our flat above a bakery. Mornings are medical-device manuals: I run them through an AI tool with my own glossary, then fix what it gets wrong, which is a lot in Arabic. Two afternoons a week I interpret at the asylum advice centre across town, and I coordinate a little group of four freelancers who share jobs so nobody undercuts anybody.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the puzzle of the tools, honestly: building a glossary so the machine stops calling a catheter a 'tube thing' in Levantine Arabic. And I like the advice centre, because it's real people. What wears me out is the per-word platforms: they pay me less every year for post-editing and pretend the machine did the work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first one is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I already say: the tools are useful helpers, not translators. I'd probably write a post for our little group saying 'see, the craft still matters', with a screenshot of the worst Arabic error from that week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me personally, not much changes, which is both good and bad. My rates were already dropping because platforms call everything 'post-editing' now. My partner Noor is on a PhD stipend, and between us we've got maybe three weeks of rent saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the tools the way I do, because they genuinely save me time on the manuals. I'd try to move our group of four off the platforms and sell directly to two or three device makers. And I'd ask the advice centre for a third afternoon a week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a familiar way. Nothing frightening, just the slow squeeze.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the platforms pretend the machine did the work. What does that look like on a payslip?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A manual that paid me eleven cents a word two years ago now pays four cents as 'post-editing'. But I still check every single line, because a wrong dose instruction in Arabic could hurt someone. The work is the same, the label changed, and the label decides my pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would going direct to device makers change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd cut out the platform's cut, which is often half. It's scary because none of us has the cushion to wait sixty days for a big company to pay. But if four of us share the risk, one late invoice doesn't sink anybody.

say: I'd say the tools are **useful helpers**, not translators.
I'd share the week's **worst Arabic error** with my freelance group.
think: My rates still fall because platforms relabel work as **post-editing**.
Noor and I have about **three weeks of rent** saved.
do: Keep using **AI tools with my glossary** on the manuals.
Move the group of four to sell **directly to device makers**.
Ask the advice centre for a **third afternoon** each week.
feel: **Uneasy** in a familiar way, feeling the **slow squeeze**.
S0.quote: The work is the same, the label changed, and the label decides my pay.
fieldNote: She uses AI daily yet resents how platforms **relabel her work** to cut pay.
Her instinct is **collective**: four freelancers sharing risk and selling direct.
Thin savings make **sixty-day payment terms** a real barrier.

steps.text: Keep running device manuals through her own AI glossary setup
Pitch two device makers directly as a group of four
Ask the asylum advice centre for a third paid afternoon

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say translators need to own the tools, not rent them from platforms. I'd push for the professional association to set rates for AI-assisted work and for clinics to require a qualified human check on medical text.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be better placed than most, because I already work this way. But the manual work would drop to maybe a quarter of the pay as clients run things through the machine themselves. My edge would be the Arabic dialect work and the medical checking, and I'd need to sell that hard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first month I'd turn our group into a proper co-op with a shared website and a name. I'd offer device makers a fixed-price 'human safety check' on machine-translated manuals. I'd also teach a paid evening workshop for other translators on building glossaries for the tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but awake. I can see a path, but I'm also living on three weeks of savings while I build it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd teach other translators the tools that might replace them. How does that sit with you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Better they learn it from someone who cares about them than from a platform's training video. If a colleague like Rasha can keep her medical clients because she's faster now, that's a win. I'd rather we all adapt together than one by one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Noor say about the co-op idea?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Noor (my partner) would ask how we pay rent in the months before the co-op earns anything. She's right to ask. I'd keep the advice centre afternoons as the steady money while I build it.

say: I'd say translators must **own the tools**, not rent them.
I'd push for a **qualified human check** on medical text.
think: I'm **better placed** than most because I already work this way.
Manual work would drop to about **a quarter** of the pay.
do: Turn the group into a **co-op** with a shared website within a month.
Offer device makers a fixed-price **human safety check**.
Teach a paid **glossary workshop** for other translators.
feel: **Anxious but awake**, seeing a path on **thin savings**.
S1.quote: Noor (my partner) would ask how we pay rent in the months before the co-op earns anything.
fieldNote: She treats disruption as a reason to **organise**, not to compete alone.
Her **dialect and medical** skills are her selling point.
The advice centre is her **steady money** while she takes risks.

steps.text: Register the four freelancers as a co-op with a shared website
Sell device makers a fixed-price human safety check on manuals
Run a paid evening glossary workshop for local translators
Keep the asylum centre afternoons as steady income

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third one is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment for public ownership of the models, or at least a tax on them to fund people's incomes. I'd be organising, not just posting. And I'd say translators were the canary in the coal mine and nobody listened.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, by 2029 a machine would translate the manuals and check them, and nobody would pay me for either. Even the dialect edge goes if it's truly as good as a person. The advice centre interpreting might last a bit, because asylum seekers need someone in the room they can trust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move fast. I'd apply for AI evaluation jobs, where they pay native Arabic speakers to test models, because that's the work that exists in the gap. I'd look for jobs in the city, where there's more of everything, and Noor and I would talk seriously about moving there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'm quick with change, but two years with three weeks of savings is not a plan, it's a sprint.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the evaluation work exists 'in the gap'. How long do you think that lasts?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe until the models stop needing people to check them, so a couple of years at most. I'd do it with my eyes open. It's rent money while I work out what's next, not a career.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The robots arrive about three years after. Does that change anything for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only for the advice centre, because being physically there with a family matters. Everything else I do is thinking work, so it's gone on the first date. If anything I'd lean harder into in-person community work, because that's where the three years are.

say: I'd call for **public ownership** of models or a tax to fund incomes.
I'd say translators were the **early warning** nobody heeded.
think: By **2029** machines would translate and check the manuals.
Only **in-person interpreting** at the advice centre might last a bit.
do: Apply for **AI evaluation** jobs testing Arabic models.
Look for work in the **city** and discuss moving with Noor.
feel: **Alarmed**: two years on three weeks of savings feels like a **sprint**.
S2.quote: Two years with three weeks of savings is not a plan, it's a sprint.
fieldNote: Even an **adaptive** translator expects to lose most income here.
She sees **evaluation work** as temporary rent money, not a career.
She'd push **public ownership** while moving fast personally.

steps.text: Apply to AI evaluation jobs that pay native Arabic speakers
Talk with Noor about moving to the city for more work
Organise local translators to campaign for a tax on AI firms

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth one is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to build something if we start now. I'd want the association, unions and the advice sector to plan together for language workers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is a real difference for me. I'd have time to move from translating into something like running language access for a hospital or the council, a job about people and systems rather than words alone. The translation income still drains away, just more slowly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the co-op going and use the tools as hard as I can while there's work. I'd do a part-time certificate in public service interpreting and health administration. And I'd put every spare euro, even thirty a month, into a separate account for the gap year I know is coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with a shape to it. I'd be busy building, which is how I cope.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd be studying, running a co-op and translating. Is that realistic on your budget?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not all at once, you're right. I'd drop the co-op admin first and let Rasha run it. The certificate matters more, because it's the bridge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you blame, if this happens?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not the technology itself. I blame the companies that will keep all the savings and the governments that let them. If AI does the work of a million translators, some of that money should pay for the million to retrain.

I'd want unions and advice services to **plan together**.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade is a gift if governments use it. Fund retraining, protect public interpreting, and make the AI companies share the gains. I'd be campaigning for that, calmly, for ten years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years means I'd be thirty-seven and probably managing language services somewhere by then. I'd ride the tools as long as they make me faster, then step into the human side. I think I'd be fine, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the co-op and translate with the tools for the next few years. In year two I'd start a part-time master's in public health or policy, aiming at a language access job. I'd also start a small paid newsletter for translators on using AI well, because people already ask me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly okay, with some unease about money while I study. It feels like weather I can see coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: A paid newsletter on top of everything. Why that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'm already answering the same three questions from colleagues every week for free. If fifty people paid three euros a month, that's my phone bill and the bus pass covered. It's small, but on our budget small matters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want to be doing in 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd like to be the person at a hospital who makes sure every patient, whatever language they speak, gets understood, with the machines doing the routine bits and humans in the hard conversations. That's still my job, just a level up.

I'd **ride the tools**, then step into the human side.

S4.quote: I'd like to be the person at a hospital who makes sure every patient, whatever language they speak, gets understood.
fieldNote: With ten years she sees a **promotion**, not an ending.

steps.text: Start a part-time public health master's in year two

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because even being quick doesn't help when the runway is two years and the savings are three weeks. What would help is a guaranteed income while people retrain, paid for by the companies making the money. And legal rules that a patient or asylum seeker always gets a human interpreter.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who teaches the machines. A lot of the Arabic these tools know came from translators like me, unpaid, through old projects scraped off the internet. I'd like that to count for something when the money is shared out.

headlineQuote: A lot of the Arabic these tools know came from translators like me, unpaid.
portrait: Fatima is a **27-year-old** German, Arabic and English translator who uses AI every day.
She coordinates **four freelancers** and lives with Noor, a PhD student, on thin savings.
She meets every scenario by **organising**: a co-op, workshops, campaigns.
She's uneasy in AI Plateau, **alarmed** by AGI in two years, and uneasy again with ten.
Her long-term aim is running **language access** for a hospital or council.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because two years and three weeks of savings leave no room.
whatWouldHelp: A **guaranteed income** during retraining, paid by AI companies.
A legal right to a **human interpreter** for patients and asylum seekers.
